claim: The alcAp-UapA-GFP/alcAp-mCherry-SynA strain grows similar to an isogenic wild-type (wt) strain in the presence of uric acid as a N source and fructose as a C source.
source: Figure 1A shows that the strain co-expressing alcAp-UapA-GFP and alcAp-mCherry-SynA grows similar to an isogenic wild-type (wt) strain in the presence of uric acid as a N source (i.e., substrate of UapA) and fructose as a C source, as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test analysis data presented in Figure 1A comparing the dual-cargo strain to wild-type.

claim: On uric acid/glucose media the alcAp-UapA-GFP/alcAp-mCherry-SynA strain resembles the ΔuapA null mutant, confirming that uapA transcription is well repressed.
source: On the other hand, on uric acid/glucose media the alcAp-UapA-GFP/alcAp-mCherry-SynA strain resembles the ΔuapA null mutant, confirming that uapA transcription is well repressed.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data in Figure 1A showing similar phenotypes between the repressed strain and the deletion mutant.

claim: Lack of SynA expression does not affect growth.
source: Notice that lack of SynA expression, either in the null mutants or in the repressible alcAp-mCherry-SynA strain, does not affect growth (see also later).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test analysis data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: UapA-GFP labels homogeneously the PM in a non-polarized or even anti-polarized manner.
source: UapA-GFP labeled homogeneously the PM in a non-polarized or even anti-polarized manner, while mCherry-SynA marked mostly the PM of the apical region of hyphae, with some overlap with UapA-GFP, at the subapical region.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing steady-state localization patterns in Figure 1B.

claim: mCherry-SynA marks mostly the PM of the apical region of hyphae.
source: UapA-GFP labeled homogeneously the PM in a non-polarized or even anti-polarized manner, while mCherry-SynA marked mostly the PM of the apical region of hyphae, with some overlap with UapA-GFP, at the subapical region.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing steady-state localization patterns in Figure 1B.

claim: UapA-GFP and mCherry-SynA show some overlap at the subapical region.
source: UapA-GFP labeled homogeneously the PM in a non-polarized or even anti-polarized manner, while mCherry-SynA marked mostly the PM of the apical region of hyphae, with some overlap with UapA-GFP, at the subapical region.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing steady-state localization patterns in Figure 1B.

claim: The two cargoes (UapA and SynA) become visible after ~60 min of initiation of transcription.
source: Widefield epifluorescence microscopy showed that in most cells the two cargoes become visible after ~60 min of initiation of transcription and progressively labeled distinct cytoplasmic compartments, before accumulating in the PM.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course microscopy data following cargo appearance after transcriptional derepression.

claim: UapA and SynA progressively label distinct cytoplasmic compartments before accumulating in the PM.
source: Widefield epifluorescence microscopy showed that in most cells the two cargoes become visible after ~60 min of initiation of transcription and progressively labeled distinct cytoplasmic compartments, before accumulating in the PM.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course microscopy data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: UapA and SynA did not seem to overlap significantly at any stage before accumulation to the PM.
source: Importantly, the two cargoes did not seem to overlap significantly at any stage before accumulation to the PM (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing distinct localization patterns in Figure 1C.

claim: Most UapA and SynA structures did not colocalize in movies recorded for a time period of 7 min (Pearson's correlation coefficient [PCC] = 0.01, n = 52).
source: The topology of UapA-labeled versus SynA-labeled structures was clearly distinct in all cells tested, as most UapA and SynA structures did not colocalize in movies recorded for a time period of 7 min (Pearson's correlation coefficient [PCC] = 0.01, n = 52).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from spinning-disc confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A small number of doubly labeled, mostly non-cortical puncta (0.33 ± 0.03 µm in diameter) were detected, suggesting that UapA and SynA might very partially colocalize on an early secretory compartment.
source: We detected only a small number of doubly labeled, mostly non-cortical puncta (0.33 ± 0.03 µm in diameter) (Figure 2A, see merged channels in middle and lower panels), suggesting that UapA and SynA might very partially colocalize on an early secretory compartment, before reaching the subapical or apical PM, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data and size measurements from Figure 2A.

claim: Both UapA and SynA structures showed low-range mobility.
source: Both UapA and SynA structures showed low-range mobility, but in addition several SynA puncta also moved toward the apical area (see Figure 2—video 3 and Figure 3—video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data from videos referenced in the text.

claim: Several SynA puncta moved toward the apical area.
source: Both UapA and SynA structures showed low-range mobility, but in addition several SynA puncta also moved toward the apical area (see Figure 2—video 3 and Figure 3—video 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by live-cell imaging data from videos referenced in the text.

claim: UapA appeared to label cytoplasmic oscillating thread structures decorated by pearl-like foci (0.32 ± 0.02 µm) as well as a very faint vesicular/tubular network.
source: In several hyphae, UapA appeared to label cytoplasmic oscillating thread structures decorated by pearl-like foci (0.32 ± 0.02 µm) as well as a very faint vesicular/tubular network (Figure 2B and associated movie in Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data and size measurements from Figure 2B and associated video.

claim: Similar thread-like structures with pearl-like foci were also seen with SynA (0.30 ± 0.03 μm).
source: Similar thread-like structures with pearl-like foci were also seen with SynA (0.30 ± 0.03 μm).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data and size measurements.

claim: Larger SynA puncta were also observed (0.52 ± 0.08 μm).
source: Larger SynA puncta were also observed (0.52 ± 0.08 μm) (Figure 2—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data and size measurements from Figure 2—video 3.

claim: The average time needed for UapA structures to move laterally toward the PM was estimated to be 12–18 s.
source: Some UapA structures were tracked moving laterally toward the PM (indicated by yellow arrow heads in Figure 2A, B, see lower left panel). The average time needed for this to occur was estimated to be 12–18 s.
evidence: The claim is supported by time-lapse microscopy data and tracking analysis from Figure 2A, B.

claim: UapA did not colocalize with the ERGIC/early-Golgi marker SedV (PCC = 0.01, n = 100).
source: Results shown in Figure 3A, B reveal that in movies recorded for a time period of 6–10 min UapA did not colocalize with any of the two Golgi markers [PCC = 0.01, n = 100 (UapA-SedV), PCC = 0.01, n = 35 (UapA-PHOSBP)]
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: UapA did not colocalize with the late-Golgi/TGN marker PHOSBP (PCC = 0.01, n = 35).
source: Results shown in Figure 3A, B reveal that in movies recorded for a time period of 6–10 min UapA did not colocalize with any of the two Golgi markers [PCC = 0.01, n = 100 (UapA-SedV), PCC = 0.01, n = 35 (UapA-PHOSBP)]
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SynA colocalized significantly with the late-Golgi marker PHOSBP (PCC = 0.74, n = 76, p < 0.0001).
source: Results shown in Figure 3A, B reveal that in movies recorded for a time period of 6–10 min UapA did not colocalize with any of the two Golgi markers [PCC = 0.01, n = 100 (UapA-SedV), PCC = 0.01, n = 35 (UapA-PHOSBP)], while SynA colocalized significantly with the late-Golgi marker PHOSBP (PCC = 0.74, n = 76, p < 0.0001), and very little with the ERGIC/early-Golgi marker SedV (PCC = 0.04, n = 40).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: SynA colocalized very little with the ERGIC/early-Golgi marker SedV (PCC = 0.04, n = 40).
source: Results shown in Figure 3A, B reveal that in movies recorded for a time period of 6–10 min UapA did not colocalize with any of the two Golgi markers [PCC = 0.01, n = 100 (UapA-SedV), PCC = 0.01, n = 35 (UapA-PHOSBP)], while SynA colocalized significantly with the late-Golgi marker PHOSBP (PCC = 0.74, n = 76, p < 0.0001), and very little with the ERGIC/early-Golgi marker SedV (PCC = 0.04, n = 40).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Significant colocalization of SynA with the late-Golgi marker PHOSBP is confirmed via Super Resolution Radial Fluctuation (SRRF) imaging.
source: Significant colocalization of SynA with the late-Golgi marker PHOSBP is also confirmed via Super Resolution Radial Fluctuation (SRRF) imaging (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by super-resolution microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SarA, Sec24, and Sec13 have been previously shown to be essential for growth.
source: Notice that SarA, Sec24, and Sec13 have been previously shown to be essential for growth, while Sec24 or Sec13 have also been found critical for proper trafficking of both polarized and non-polarized cargoes (Hernández-González et al., 2015; Dimou et al., 2022; Dimou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sec24 or Sec13 have been found critical for proper trafficking of both polarized and non-polarized cargoes.
source: Notice that SarA, Sec24, and Sec13 have been previously shown to be essential for growth, while Sec24 or Sec13 have also been found critical for proper trafficking of both polarized and non-polarized cargoes (Hernández-González et al., 2015; Dimou et al., 2022; Dimou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed that SarA, Sec24, Sec13, and Sec31 could be tightly repressed.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that we could tightly repress the expression of SarA, Sec24, Sec13, and Sec31 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Sec12 could not be detected in western blots, probably due to an apparent high turnover or modification of its terminal regions.
source: Sec12 could not be detected in western blots, probably due to an apparent high turnover or modification of its terminal regions.
evidence: The claim is based on the inability to detect Sec12 in western blots and speculation about the reason.

claim: Thiamine repression of COPII-related genes led to lack (sarA, sec24, sec13, or sec31) or dramatically reduced (sec12) colony growth in the respective strains.
source: As expected, thiamine repression of COPII-related genes led to lack (sarA, sec24, sec13, or sec31) or dramatically reduced (sec12) colony growth in the respective strains (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Repression of SarA, Sec24, Sec31, and Sec13 led to total retention of SynA at the ER network in ~100% of cells.
source: Repression of SarA, Sec24, Sec31, and Sec13 led to total retention of SynA at the ER network in ~100% of cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SynA localization upon COPII component repression in Figure 4C.

claim: UapA trafficking was totally blocked upon SarA or Sec31 repression (100% of cells).
source: UapA trafficking was also totally blocked upon SarA or Sec31 repression (100% of cells), and also efficiently blocked when Sec24 was repressed (~76% of cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization upon COPII component repression in Figure 4C.

claim: UapA trafficking was efficiently blocked when Sec24 was repressed (~76% of cells).
source: UapA trafficking was also totally blocked upon SarA or Sec31 repression (100% of cells), and also efficiently blocked when Sec24 was repressed (~76% of cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization upon COPII component repression in Figure 4C.

claim: UapA trafficking was not efficiently blocked upon Sec13 repression in most samples (~80% of cells).
source: Interestingly, UapA trafficking to the PM was not efficiently blocked upon Sec13 repression in most samples (~80% of cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization upon Sec13 repression in Figure 4C.

claim: UapA-mediated xanthine transport was very low when Sec24 was repressed (~15% of wt).
source: Figure 4D shows that UapA-mediated xanthine transport was very low when Sec24 was repressed (~15% of wt) but remained relatively high when Sec13 was repressed (~72% of wt or non-repressed levels).
evidence: The claim is supported by radiolabeled xanthine transport assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: UapA-mediated xanthine transport remained relatively high when Sec13 was repressed (~72% of wt).
source: Figure 4D shows that UapA-mediated xanthine transport was very low when Sec24 was repressed (~15% of wt) but remained relatively high when Sec13 was repressed (~72% of wt or non-repressed levels).
evidence: The claim is supported by radiolabeled xanthine transport assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Sec12 repression led to a moderate negative effect on the trafficking of both UapA and SynA to the PM (~33–38%, n = 116, t = 4).
source: Finally, Sec12 repression of transcription was shown to lead to a moderate negative effect on the trafficking of both UapA and SynA to the PM (~33–38%, n = 116, t = 4), compatible with a less profound effect on growth (see Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization upon Sec12 repression in Figure 4C.

claim: The sec31ts-AP mutation showed a thermosensitive growth phenotype at 42°C.
source: We constructed several A. nidulans Sec31 mutant strains (see Materials and methods) and identified one that showed a thermosensitive growth phenotype at 42°C (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: At the restrictive temperature (42°C), both UapA and SynA fail to reach the PM in the sec31ts-AP strain.
source: As shown in Figure 5B (left panel), when spore germination takes place at 42°C, both cargoes fail to reach the PM, as expected given the essentiality of Sec31, shown also earlier in this work (see Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization at restrictive temperature in Figure 5B.

claim: UapA and SynA marked very distinct areas of a membranous network typical of the ER at 42°C in the sec31ts-AP strain.
source: Importantly, UapA and SynA marked very distinct areas of a membranous network typical of the ER (see merged panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization at restrictive temperature in Figure 5B.

claim: When cells were shifted from 42 to 25°C, both UapA and SynA progressively marked puncta on or closely associated with the ER membranous network.
source: When cells were shifted from 42 to 25°C and observed after 0–45 min, the picture changed (Figure 5B, right panel). More specifically, both cargoes progressively marked puncta on or closely associated with the ER membranous network, often associated with rings reflecting nuclear ER, but also in cortical regions next to the PM.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization after temperature shift in Figure 5B.

claim: UapA and SynA puncta did not colocalize significantly after temperature shift (PCC = 0.28 ± 0.06, n = 17).
source: Most notably, UapA and SynA puncta did not colocalize significantly (PCC = 0.28 ± 0.06, n = 17).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data in Figure 5B.

claim: Both UapA and SynA exhibited significant colocalization with the ERES marker Sec16 (PCC = 0.66 ± 0.08, n = 22 UapA-Sec16; PCC = 0.58 ± 0.09, n = 37 SynA-Sec16).
source: Figure 5C shows the localization of UapA-GFP/Sec16-mCherry or GFP-SynA/Sec16-mCherry in the presence of sec31ts mutation after growth in a non-permissive temperature (42°C) and transfer to permissive temperature (25°C). Both cargoes show significant colocalization with Sec16 (PCC ≈ 0.6) in clearly defined puncta, as those detected in Figure 5B.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Repression of either CopA or ArfA abolished translocation of UapA and SynA to the PM.
source: As shown in Figure 5D, repression of either CopA or ArfA, abolished translocation of these cargoes to the PM.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization upon CopA or ArfA repression in Figure 5D.

claim: Upon CopA repression, UapA and SynA collapse in distinct internal structures with little colocalization (PCC = 0.15 ± 0.08, n = 9).
source: Noticeably, the picture obtained upon CopA repression was rather similar to what has been observed when cargo trafficking was followed in the background of the sec31ts strain shifted from 42 to 25°C. More specifically, we observed distinct, little colocalizing (PCC = 0.15 ± 0.08, n = 9), UapA or SynA cytosolic puncta associated with the ER network.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Upon ArfA repression, UapA is sorted into vacuoles and SynA collapses all over the ER membrane with distinct structures (PCC = −0.14 ± 0.1, n = 10).
source: On the other hand, upon ArfA repression, the effect on cargo trafficking seemed more dramatic compared to CopA repression or sec31ts, with UapA sorted into vacuoles and SynA collapsed all over the ER membrane. This might be related to the fact the ArfA has a pleiotropic effect on other steps in cargo trafficking, besides recruitment of COPI. Notably, the ER membranes where SynA collapses upon ArfA repression is distinct from the structures marked with UapA (PCC = −0.14 ± 0.1, n = 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative colocalization analysis using Pearson's correlation coefficient from microscopy data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Repression of SedV, GeaA, RabO, RabE, or AP-1σ led to total failure of SynA to accumulate in the PM of the apical region in all cells.
source: Our results showed that in all cells repressed for SedV, GeaA, RabO, RabE, or AP-1σ, and ~60% of cells repressed for HypB, SynA totally failed to accumulate in the PM of the apical region, and instead labeled cytoplasmic foci or large aggregates.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SynA localization upon Golgi protein repression in Figure 6C.

claim: In ~60% of cells repressed for HypB, SynA totally failed to accumulate in the PM of the apical region.
source: Our results showed that in all cells repressed for SedV, GeaA, RabO, RabE, or AP-1σ, and ~60% of cells repressed for HypB, SynA totally failed to accumulate in the PM of the apical region, and instead labeled cytoplasmic foci or large aggregates.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SynA localization upon HypB repression in Figure 6C.

claim: In GeaA, HypB, RabO, or AP-1σ repressible strains UapA translocation to the PM was practically unaffected in all cells (~100%).
source: In contrast to SynA, UapA translocated to the PM when several key Golgi proteins were repressed. More specifically, in GeaA, HypB, RabO, or AP-1σ repressible strains UapA translocation to the PM was practically unaffected in all cells (~100%).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization upon Golgi protein repression in Figure 6C.

claim: Repression of SedV led to a block in UapA trafficking to the PM in ~65% of cells.
source: Repression of SedV led to a block in UapA trafficking to the PM in ~65% of cells, while in ~35% of cells UapA was normally localized to the PM.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization upon SedV repression in Figure 6C.

claim: Upon RabE repression, a significant fraction of UapA could translocate to the PM in ~75% of cells, but the same cells also showed numerous large cytoplasmic structures.
source: Upon RabE repression, a significant fraction of UapA could translocate to the PM in ~75% of cells, but in this case, the same cells also showed numerous large cytoplasmic structures.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization upon RabE repression in Figure 6C.

claim: UapA transport activity was high when HypB or Ap1σ were repressed (83–100% of wt).
source: As shown in Figure 6D, we detected high levels of UapA activity (i.e., transport of radiolabeled xanthine) in strains repressed for HypB and AP-1σ (83–100% of the transport rate of wt), whereas transport activity was reduced to 27% and 19% of the wt when RabE and SedV were repressed, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by radiolabeled xanthine transport assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: UapA transport activity was reduced to 27% of wt when RabE was repressed.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, we detected high levels of UapA activity (i.e., transport of radiolabeled xanthine) in strains repressed for HypB and AP-1σ (83–100% of the transport rate of wt), whereas transport activity was reduced to 27% and 19% of the wt when RabE and SedV were repressed, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by radiolabeled xanthine transport assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: UapA transport activity was reduced to 19% of wt when SedV was repressed.
source: As shown in Figure 6D, we detected high levels of UapA activity (i.e., transport of radiolabeled xanthine) in strains repressed for HypB and AP-1σ (83–100% of the transport rate of wt), whereas transport activity was reduced to 27% and 19% of the wt when RabE and SedV were repressed, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by radiolabeled xanthine transport assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Addition of BFA for 60 min after derepression of cargoes blocks the trafficking of SynA in all cells (~100%).
source: Our results showed that addition of BFA for 60 min after derepression of cargoes for 90 min, blocks the trafficking of SynA in all cells (~100%), leading to the trapping of this cargo into large Golgi aggregates (known as 'brefeldin bodies'), but has only a very modest effect on UapA translocation to the PM (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization upon BFA treatment in Figure 6E.

claim: Addition of BFA has only a very modest effect on UapA translocation to the PM.
source: Our results showed that addition of BFA for 60 min after derepression of cargoes for 90 min, blocks the trafficking of SynA in all cells (~100%), leading to the trapping of this cargo into large Golgi aggregates (known as 'brefeldin bodies'), but has only a very modest effect on UapA translocation to the PM (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization upon BFA treatment in Figure 6E.

claim: Proper trafficking of SynA to the apical PM was totally abolished by benomyl treatment.
source: Our results showed that proper trafficking of SynA to the apical PM was totally abolished, as expected for a conventional cargo, while UapA translocates normally to the PM, in all cells, similar to the control without benomyl (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization upon benomyl treatment in Figure 6F.

claim: UapA translocates normally to the PM upon benomyl treatment, in all cells.
source: Our results showed that proper trafficking of SynA to the apical PM was totally abolished, as expected for a conventional cargo, while UapA translocates normally to the PM, in all cells, similar to the control without benomyl (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization upon benomyl treatment in Figure 6F.

claim: In S. cerevisiae, the SNARE proteins Sed5, Bos1, Bet1, and Sec22 form a basic trans-SNARE complex required for vesicular traffic from the ER to the Golgi apparatus.
source: In S. cerevisiae, the SNARE proteins Sed5, Bos1, Bet1, and Sec22 have been shown to form a basic trans-SNARE complex required for vesicular traffic from the ER to the Golgi apparatus (Shim et al., 1991; Dascher et al., 1991; Hardwick and Pelham, 1992; Parlati et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in S. cerevisiae.

claim: Two additional yeast SNAREs, Ykt6 and Sft1, play essential roles in cargo trafficking via their interaction with Sed5 at the ER–Golgi interface.
source: Importantly, two additional yeast SNAREs, Ykt6 and Sft1, have also been shown to play essential roles in cargo trafficking via their interaction with Sed5 at the ER–Golgi interface (Kweon et al., 2003; Adnan et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Strains carrying thiAp-sft1 and thiAp-ykt6 alleles could not form colonies in the presence of thiamine but grew normally in the absence of thiamine.
source: Strains carrying thiAp-sft1 and thiAp-ykt6 alleles could not form colonies in the presence of thiamine but grew normally in the absence of thiamine.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The Δsec22 mutant and thiAp-bos1 and thiAp-bet1 strains showed a significant growth defect under repressed conditions, but less prominent compared to that where Ykt6 or Sft1 were repressed.
source: The Δsec22 mutant and thiAp-bos1 and thiAp-bet1 strains also showed a significant growth defect under repressed conditions, but less prominent compared to that where Ykt6 or Sft1 were repressed (Figure 7A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: SynA proper trafficking was severely mitigated in ~100% of cells upon repression of Sft1 or Ykt6.
source: SynA proper trafficking was severely mitigated in ~100% of cells upon repression of Sft1 or Ykt6, while it was little affected when Bet1 was repressed (reduced accumulation at the apex), and not affected when Bos1 was repressed or in the Δsec22 mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SynA localization upon SNARE repression in Figure 7B.

claim: SynA trafficking was little affected when Bet1 was repressed (reduced accumulation at the apex).
source: SynA proper trafficking was severely mitigated in ~100% of cells upon repression of Sft1 or Ykt6, while it was little affected when Bet1 was repressed (reduced accumulation at the apex), and not affected when Bos1 was repressed or in the Δsec22 mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SynA localization upon SNARE repression in Figure 7B.

claim: SynA trafficking was not affected when Bos1 was repressed or in the Δsec22 mutant.
source: SynA proper trafficking was severely mitigated in ~100% of cells upon repression of Sft1 or Ykt6, while it was little affected when Bet1 was repressed (reduced accumulation at the apex), and not affected when Bos1 was repressed or in the Δsec22 mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SynA localization upon SNARE repression in Figure 7B.

claim: UapA trafficking to the PM was not affected in any of the five SNARE mutants tested (Ykt6, Sft1, Bet1, Bos1, Sec22).
source: Most importantly, UapA trafficking to the PM was not affected in any of the five SNARE mutants tested.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization upon SNARE repression in Figure 7B.

claim: SynA proper trafficking was abolished in Δsec22 thiAp-ykt6 double mutant.
source: As expected, SynA proper trafficking was abolished in Δsec22 thiAp-ykt6, but still UapA translocation to the PM remained unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing SynA localization in the double mutant in Figure 7B.

claim: UapA translocation to the PM remained unaffected in Δsec22 thiAp-ykt6 double mutant.
source: As expected, SynA proper trafficking was abolished in Δsec22 thiAp-ykt6, but still UapA translocation to the PM remained unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing UapA localization in the double mutant in Figure 7B.

claim: In yeast, vesicular fusion to the PM occurs via the action of the hetero-octameric exocyst complex and the trans-interaction of Qa/b-SNAREs Sso1/2 and Sec9 with vesicular R-SNAREs Snc1/Snc2.
source: In yeast, this occurs via the action of the hetero-octameric exocyst complex (a tethering complex) and the trans-interaction of Qa/b-SNAREs Sso1/2 and Sec9 with vesicular R-SNAREs Snc1/Snc2 (Couve and Gerst, 1994; Katz and Brennwald, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies in yeast.

claim: The ΔsynA mutant showed only a minor growth defect at alkaline pH at 25°C.
source: Surprisingly, unlike the double deleted Δsnc1Δsnc2 yeast mutant, which is inviable, the ΔsynA mutant showed only a minor growth defect at alkaline pH at 25°C (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Strains harboring thiAp-sec9 or thiAp-ssoA alleles could not form colonies on a Petri dish supplemented with thiamine.
source: On the other hand, strains harboring thiAp-sec9 or thiAp-ssoA alleles could not form colonies on a Petri dish supplemented with thiamine (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed that the expression of Sec9 could be tightly repressed in the presence of thiamine.
source: Western blot analysis confirmed that the expression of Sec9 could be tightly repressed in the presence of thiamine (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The deletion of rabD (ΔrabD) had a prominent morphological defect coupled with altered colony morphology.
source: Finally, the deletion of rabD (ΔrabD) had a prominent morphological defect coupled with altered colony morphology, as also previously described by others (Pantazopoulou et al., 2014; Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test data shown in Figure 8A and citation to previous work.

claim: Repression of SsoA or Sec9 blocked the translocation of both ChsB and UapA to the PM.
source: Live cell imagining showed that repression of SsoA or Sec9 (Figure 8C) blocked the translocation of both ChsB and UapA to the PM, as these cargoes marked cytoplasmic puncta.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization upon SsoA or Sec9 repression in Figure 8C.

claim: Both ChsB and UapA reached the PM normally in the ΔsynA mutant.
source: In contrast, both cargoes reached the PM normally in the ΔsynA mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization in the ΔsynA mutant in Figure 8C.

claim: The ΔnyvA null mutation did not affect growth and has not affected trafficking of UapA or ChsB.
source: However, the ΔnyvA null mutation did not affect growth and has not affected trafficking of UapA or ChsB.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth test and microscopy data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The triple combination of ΔnyvA ΔsynA Δsec22 did not affect neither UapA nor ChsB trafficking to the PM.
source: To further test a possible additive or compensatory role of different v-SNARES, we also constructed and tested the triple combination of ΔnyvA ΔsynA Δsec22. The combination of these three R-SNAREs did not affect neither UapA nor ChsB trafficking to the PM (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization in the triple mutant in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the ΔrabD strain, UapA localization to the PM was not affected, while SynA translocation to the apical PM was significantly blocked.
source: Lastly, in the strain deleted for RabD (ΔrabD) UapA localization to the PM was not affected, while SynA translocation to the apical PM (or that of ChsB; not shown) was significantly blocked (Figure 8D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data showing cargo localization in the ΔrabD strain in Figure 8D.

claim: SynA has been shown to localize polarly in the apex of growing hyphae via conventional Golgi and post-Golgi secretion.
source: In these studies, SynA has been shown to localize polarly in the apex of growing hyphae via conventional Golgi and post-Golgi secretion (Taheri-Talesh et al., 2008; Martzoukou et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: UapA localized non-polarly all over the hyphal PM, through a mechanism that essentially did not require Golgi maturation and post-Golgi secretion.
source: whereas UapA localized non-polarly all over the hyphal PM, through a mechanism that essentially did not require Golgi maturation and post-Golgi secretion (Dimou et al., 2020; Dimou et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Derepression of alcAp by fructose leads to medium levels of expression.
source: Derepression of alcAp by fructose leads to medium levels of expression (Flipphi et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The partial independence of UapA localization on sec24 repression might be due to the existence of a Sec24 homolog, namely LstA, in A. nidulans.
source: The partial independence of UapA localization on sec24 repression might be due to the existence of a Sec24 homolog, namely LstA, in A. nidulans (Dimou et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the partial effect of Sec24 repression and citation to previous work identifying LstA.

claim: LstA is known to function as a cargo selection adaptor, similar to Sec24, for bulky or large oligomeric cargoes.
source: LstA is known to function as a cargo selection adaptor, similar to Sec24, for bulky or large oligomeric cargoes (Dimou et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: UapA is a large cargo (the UapA dimer has 28 transmembrane segments).
source: Notice that UapA is indeed a large cargo (i.e., the UapA dimer has 28 transmembrane segments), while SynA is a relatively small cargo (single transmembrane segment).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the structure of UapA.

claim: SynA is a relatively small cargo (single transmembrane segment).
source: Notice that UapA is indeed a large cargo (i.e., the UapA dimer has 28 transmembrane segments), while SynA is a relatively small cargo (single transmembrane segment).
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the structure of SynA.

claim: Sec13 has been shown to serve the rigidification of the COPII cage, which in turn leads to an increase in its membrane-bending capacity.
source: Most notably, Sec13 has been shown, through both genetic and biochemical approaches, to serve the rigidification of the COPII cage, which in turn leads to an increase in its membrane-bending capacity, especially needed when specific cargoes tend to elicit the opposing curvature toward the lumen of the ER (Copic et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A requirement for Sec13 can be bypassed when non-essential membrane cargo proteins are depleted (e.g., GPIs or p24-family proteins).
source: Interestingly, a requirement for Sec13 can also be bypassed when non-essential membrane cargo proteins are depleted (e.g., GPIs or p24-family proteins). These proteins cause a concave negative curvature of the membrane into the ER lumen, which to be inverted necessitates Sec13 (D'Arcangelo et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: UapA is known to form a tight dimer, necessary for its transport activity.
source: UapA is known to form a tight dimer, necessary for its transport activity, and genetic evidence suggests that UapA dimers might further oligomerize to achieve concentrative exit from the ER (Martzoukou et al., 2015; Kourkoulou et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genetic evidence suggests that UapA dimers might further oligomerize to achieve concentrative exit from the ER.
source: UapA is known to form a tight dimer, necessary for its transport activity, and genetic evidence suggests that UapA dimers might further oligomerize to achieve concentrative exit from the ER (Martzoukou et al., 2015; Kourkoulou et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fungal nutrient transporters, unlike those of mammals, are not glycosylated.
source: Furthermore, in line with Golgi-bypass, fungal nutrient transporters, unlike those of mammals, are not glycosylated (Zielinska et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The trafficking of Chs1, a chitin synthase localized in growing hyphal tips but also in nascent septa and subapical spherical structures in Neurospora crassa, has been found to be unaffected upon Benomyl and BFA treatment.
source: Noticeably also, the trafficking of Chs1, a chitin synthase localized in growing hyphal tips but also in nascent septa and subapical spherical structures in the filamentous fungus Neurospora crassa has been found to be unaffected upon Benomyl and BFA treatment, which suggests a Golgi-bypass mechanism (Sánchez-León et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: In A. nidulans transporters and apical cargoes use different endocytic mechanisms for their internalization, turnover or recycling.
source: Notice also that in A. nidulans transporters and apical cargoes use different endocytic mechanisms for their internalization, turnover or recycling (Martzoukou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There are reports showing that the 3Q:1R ratio might not be necessary for the formation of a trans-SNARE complex.
source: Interestingly, there are reports showing that the 3Q:1R ratio might not be necessary the formation of a trans-SNARE complex. In these studies, genetic and biochemical assays have shown that SNARE complexes composed of four glutamines (4Q) are fully functional for assembly in vitro and exocytic function in vivo.
evidence: The claim is based on reference to previous studies showing alternative SNARE complex compositions.

claim: SNARE complexes may be composed entirely of Q-SNAREs in non-canonical, context-dependent, combinations, for the trafficking of specific cargoes or under specific conditions.
source: Thus, SNARE complexes may, in principle, be composed entirely of Q-SNAREs in non-canonical, context-dependent, combinations, for the trafficking of specific cargoes or under specific conditions (Katz and Brennwald, 2000; Ossig et al., 2000; Parlati et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some SNAREs, like Sed5, are known to possess remarkable plasticity in mediating distinct trans-SNARE complexes.
source: In line with this, some SNAREs, like Sed5, are known to possess remarkable plasticity in mediating distinct trans-SNARE complexes (D'Souza et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Hyperactive Sly1 can directly tether close-range vesicles with high curvature to the Qa-SNARE on the target organelle.
source: Most interestingly, in a recent article it has been shown that hyperactive Sly1, a member of the Sec1/mammalian Unc-18 (SM) family of SNARE chaperones, can directly tether close-range vesicles with high curvature to the Qa-SNARE on the target organelle (Duan et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: In Trichoderma reesei, growing apical and non-growing subapical hyphal compartments possess spatially distinct ternary SNARE complexes at their PM, involving two SsoA-like paralogs (SSOI and SSOII) interacting with their SynA-like partner (SNCI).
source: Notice also that in the filamentous fungus Trichoderma reesei growing apical and non-growing subapical hyphal compartments have been shown to possess spatially distinct ternary SNARE complexes at their PM, involving two SsoA-like paralogs (SSOI and SSOII) interacting with their SynA-like partner (SNCI). This finding indicated that there is more than one pathway for exocytosis in filamentous fungi, employing different surface SNARE proteins, at apical and subapical regions of fungal cells (Valkonen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study in T. reesei.

claim: Distinct exocytic routes in apical and subapical regions have been suggested in older studies in filamentous fungi.
source: Distinct exocytic routes in apical and subapical regions have also been suggested in older studies in filamentous fungi (Harsay and Bretscher, 1995; Nykanen et al., 1997; Davis et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Secretion of the non-polarized GPI-anchored protein EglC to the cell periphery and septa was little impaired in the absence of RabD.
source: Previous findings on the tethering role of the exocyst complex in A. nidulans showed that, similar to UapA, secretion of the non-polarized GPI-anchored protein EglC to the cell periphery and septa was little impaired in the absence of RabD (Peñalva et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Fungal exocyst proteins and associated effectors are polarly localized.
source: Notice also that while fungal exocyst proteins and associated effectors (e.g., Sec4 or Sec1) are polarly localized, the functionally relevant transmembrane SNARE SsoA is distributed all along the PM, despite a relatively higher abundance in the apical membrane (Martzoukou et al., 2018; Dimou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The transmembrane SNARE SsoA is distributed all along the PM, despite a relatively higher abundance in the apical membrane.
source: Notice also that while fungal exocyst proteins and associated effectors (e.g., Sec4 or Sec1) are polarly localized, the functionally relevant transmembrane SNARE SsoA is distributed all along the PM, despite a relatively higher abundance in the apical membrane (Martzoukou et al., 2018; Dimou et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Distinct ERES generating specific COPII subpopulations have been shown to be formed in vitro and in vivo for specific glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins or other cargoes, such as hexose or amino acid transporters.
source: Distinct ERES generating specific COPII subpopulations have been shown to be formed in vitro and in vivo for specific glycosyl-phosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins or other cargoes, such as hexose or amino acid transporters (Muñiz et al., 2001; Watanabe et al., 2008; Castillon et al., 2009; Castillon et al., 2011; Rodriguez-Gallardo et al., 2021), but also interleukin-1b (Zhang et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A Rab1-dependent, Golgi-independent, pathway connecting directly a pre-Golgi IC with the PM has been reported in polarized neuroendocrine PC12 cells.
source: Most interestingly, a Rab1-dependent, Golgi-independent, pathway connecting directly a pre-Golgi IC with the PM has been reported in polarized neuroendocrine PC12 cells (Sannerud et al., 2006; Saraste and Marie, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two types of ERGIC subpopulations have been identified in plants: one forms a dynamic reticulated tubulo-vesicular network generated independently from Golgi maturation, while the other is more stable, more cisterna-like, and dependent on Golgi.
source: In fact, distinct early secretory ICs have been reported in plants, where two types of ERGIC-type subpopulations have been identified (Fougère et al., 2023). One subpopulation forms a dynamic reticulated tubulo-vesicular network, generated independently from Golgi maturation, while the other subpopulation is more stable, more cisterna-like, and dependent on Golgi.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study in plants.
